profile.campus: Red Oak Campus, Compass Datacenters Dallas-Fort Worth market
profile.address: Ellis County, TX (Red Oak development campus, westernmost row, north end)
profile.reading: This OpenStreetMap record is one of eleven adjacent building footprints in Compass Datacenters Red Oak development, a wholesale data center campus in Ellis County, Texas, just south of the Dallas-Fort Worth core. This particular footprint sits in the westernmost row of the campus, the northernmost of five buildings arranged along that row. Compass Datacenters own market materials describe this campus, part of its Dallas-Fort Worth market, as a 360 megawatt development that was still nearing completion as of the most recent site content reviewed, with a confirmed 200 million dollar expansion phase announced in April 2024 that added two buildings totaling more than 500,000 square feet. A separate July 2026 company news item states that Red Oak now hosts seven data centers total, though that figure appears to describe the city of Red Oak as a whole rather than Compass own building count specifically, so it should not be read as confirming exactly how many of the eleven OpenStreetMap footprints in this cluster are Compass-operated versus operated by other companies also active in the area. Compass Datacenters was founded in 2011 by Chris Crosby, a former Digital Realty senior executive who remains the company CEO, and completed its first data center, a 1.2 megawatt facility, in 2012. The company is headquartered in Dallas, Texas, and describes its current ownership, per its own about-us page, as Ontario Teachers Pension Plan, RedBird Capital Partners, and company management. Beyond Dallas-Fort Worth, Compass 2026 markets list includes active developments in Chicago Hoffman Estates, Northern Virginia Loudoun County, Toronto, and Milan, plus a newly broken-ground site in Meridian, Mississippi, alongside earlier markets including Minneapolis and Nashville that the company has since exited or transferred to independent ownership. Separately, Compass donated 12.6 million dollars to fund a 40,000 square foot workforce-training replica data center at 300 Houston School Road in Red Oak, operated by Texas State Technical College, a distinct facility from the wholesale buildings mapped here that should not be confused with them. No per-building capacity, square footage, tenant, or year-built figure could be confirmed for this specific structure within the campus, and no local government permit or tax-abatement record could be retrieved this session, so those figures are deliberately omitted rather than estimated from the campus-wide totals above.

reading.body:
The Compass Red Oak Campus in Ellis County, Texas is a major hyperscale buildout whose published capacity is not confirmed. The operator announced in 2020 a target of over 350 MW of IT load on a 225-acre site, with subsequent expansions bringing the approved footprint to roughly 830 acres as of May 2026. At a conservative 10 MW per large hyperscale building, a completed 1 million square foot facility represents roughly 10 MW, and named projects targeting 1.25 million square feet combined suggest 125 MW in that phase alone, though no single current operating capacity figure was found in published sources.

This campus ranks below Texas's 18 facilities with published megawatt figures, and the state's total published capacity of 468 MW across all mapped facilities means Texas's AI infrastructure remains concentrated among a small set of announced sites. Compass operates approximately 17 data centers across the US, Canada, and Israel, making this one site within a geographically distributed operator, not a single point of infrastructure concentration.

The campus carries both scale trajectory and community friction. Local opposition to the 830-acre expansion proposal gathered over 2,200 signatures, and Compass responded with commitments to Ellis County including a 15 million dollar animal shelter grant and a technician training partnership with Texas State Technical College. The site's binding constraint status depends entirely on the power infrastructure available to it, which the published specifications do not address.
